images.filename: "A Mother's Hands" - Monument Dedicated to the Armenian Genocide.jpg
images.caption:
"A Mother's Hands" - Monument Dedicated to the Armenian Genocide
Artist: Daniel Varoujan Hejinian (2014)
This genocide memorial is to not acknowledge the killing of 1.5 million people from 1915 to 1923 and is the first Armenian Genocide monument unveiled on the site of a government building in the U.S.The monument is made of bronze and granite and there are two three-dimensional hands at the top of the piece of art showing a mother's hands crocheting.  At the bottom of the structure is inscribed the words "In Memory" both in English and Armenian.

Location: 375 Merrimack Street (outside City Hall)

images.filename: Arn Chorn-Pond sings at Lowell MA Water Festival 1999.jpg
images.caption: Lowell, Massachusetts.  August, 1999.  Arn Chorn-Pond took to the stage at the 1999 Water Festival in Lowell, MA.  The stage presence that made him an international speaker for children's rights and cultural survival also comes through when he sings.  The Khmer Rouge thoroughly destroyed the world of Cambodian opera that was Arn's family's business for generations.  Nevertheless, Arn inherited enough musical ability to stay alive by playing for the soldiers.  Now he is often happiest when singing the classic 1960s songs of the Sen Sisamouth.
images.alt: Lowell, Massachusetts.  August, 1999.  Arn Chorn-Pond took to the stage at the 1999 Water Festival in Lowell, MA.  The stage presence that made him an international speaker for children's rights and cultural survival also comes through when he sings.  The Khmer Rouge thoroughly destroyed the world of Cambodian opera that was Arn's family's business for generations.  Nevertheless, Arn inherited enough musical ability to stay alive by playing for the soldiers.  Now he is often happiest when singing the classic 1960s songs of the Sen Sisamouth.

images.filename: Bin Phan and Arn Chorn-Pond play at Lowell Water Festival 1997.jpg
images.caption: Lowell, Massachusetts. August 1997.  Arn Chorn-Pond and Cambodian Master Musician Bin Phan perform together at the Lowell Water Festival in 1997.  The khim is Cambodia's traditional hammered dulcimer, and it saved Arn's life in Khmer Rouge work camps when he was a child.  In the labor camp for 500 children, the Khmer Rouge soldiers asked for volunteers to learn music from an old master teacher.   After a week, they chose the two best students and executed the old master.  Arn had to watch the old man die and never knew his name, but stayed alive for the next few years playing khim for the soldiers.  He later learned to play the bamboo flute, or kloy, and used it when speaking until he became known as "The Flute Player".
